subject: Science
title: Global warming and choices
objective_verbatim: Describe causes and effects of global warming and how to reduce our impact.
reading_age_est: rough ARI grade 5.66 on 826 pupil-visible words; heuristic age guide 11.66 years, not a formal reading-age test
pupil_words: explain a cause and an effect of global warming, then compare two kinds of action.
success_criteria: I can put cause before effect.
I can say how gases add to warming.
I can compare a cut in emissions with help for an impact.

vocab.definition: the pattern of weather over many years
vocab.example: Climate is not the weather on one day.

vocab.definition: a gas added to the air when fossil fuels burn
vocab.example: Burning coal adds carbon dioxide to the air.

vocab.definition: a gas in the air that slows heat leaving Earth
vocab.example: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas.

vocab.definition: an effect on people or places
vocab.example: More heat can have an impact on people.

retrieval.question: Name one fact about the Solar System and its class card.
retrieval.answer: The Sun is a star, on card A; or Earth goes round the Sun, on card B.

retrieval.question: Why does one place have night?
retrieval.answer: Earth turns so that place faces away from sunlight.

retrieval.question: Name one way friction can affect motion.
retrieval.answer: It can slow a moving object.

stages.pupil_text: Sort these: weather today; climate over many years. Point to the long-term idea.
stages.adult_text: Offer a predictable seat or standing spot and the first visual cue. No public test.

stages.pupil_text: Think back. Say, point or write one answer for each question.
stages.adult_text: Ask three low-stakes retrieval questions; prior coverage must be checked.

stages.pupil_text: I order the chain: burn fuel → more carbon dioxide → more heat stays → warming. Cutting emissions acts near the start. A flood defence helps with an impact.
stages.adult_text: Model the full reasoning step, pre-teach four words and ask the show-me question.

stages.pupil_text: The burn fuel and impact cards are in place. Sort the missing gas and warming cards. Explain the link.
stages.adult_text: Show the part-done example, then allow paired talk before an answer. One-minute reset inside this stage.

stages.pupil_text: Choose what follows burning more fossil fuel in our warming chain. Everyone answers together.
stages.adult_text: All pupils answer the four-option hinge; use the decision rule, not a score.

stages.pupil_text: Build a cause-to-impact chain. Compare an emissions cut with help for an impact. Give one reason for each.
stages.adult_text: One adult supports agreed pupils, the other holds the group; swap across the week. One-minute reset inside this stage.

stages.pupil_text: Hear feedback. Move one chain card and say why.
stages.adult_text: Give a specific verbal comment (VF) and invite one self-edit (//) or read-back (?).

stages.pupil_text: Name a cause, an effect and an action. Which link does your action change?
stages.adult_text: Hear the answer and name how it changes the next example or support. One-minute reset and handoff.

worked_example.full: Burn fossil fuel → add carbon dioxide → more heat stays → heat risks. Cut fuel use to cut emissions; plan shade to help with heat.
worked_example.faded: Burn fuel → add carbon dioxide → ____ → heat risks.
worked_example.removed_step: Explain that greenhouse gases slow heat leaving Earth.
worked_example.fade_next: Next time omit the gas card and ask pupils to choose both middle links from a mixed set.

cfu.question: Point to the cause card: burning fuel or a hotter day?
cfu.answer: Burning fuel is the cause card; a hotter day may be an effect.

hinge.question: A bus depot burns more diesel. Which immediate link belongs in its emissions chain?

options.text: The extra carbon dioxide appears only when the depot has less daylight.
options.diagnosis: Makes the emissions depend on daylight instead of fuel burnt.

options.text: The depot warms first; that warmth makes its engines release carbon dioxide.
options.diagnosis: Reverses the chain: warming follows added greenhouse gases, rather than causing this exhaust.

options.text: Only local air pollution changes; the amount of carbon dioxide stays the same.
options.diagnosis: Confuses a local air-quality effect with the absence of carbon-dioxide emissions.

hinge.decision_rule: About 3 in 4 or more right → move on. Otherwise re-model with the named I-do example, then ask the parallel hinge.
hinge.parallel_hinge: Third case: a building burns less gas for heat. What changes first in this simplified chain? Answer: less carbon dioxide from burning that gas, all else equal.

misconceptions.misconception: Less daylight controls whether diesel exhaust releases carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.spot: Pupil chooses B, making emissions depend on daylight.
misconceptions.correction: Trace the immediate fuel-burning step regardless of daylight.

misconceptions.misconception: Diesel exhaust only changes local air quality and adds no carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.spot: Pupil chooses D, treating local pollution as the only diesel effect.
misconceptions.correction: Separate local air-quality effects from the added greenhouse gas.

we_do.support: Lay the first and last cards; point to each missing space before choosing a card.
we_do.stretch: Explain why a flood defence does not remove carbon dioxide already added by burning fuel.
we_do.F: Lay the first and last cards; point to each missing space before choosing a card.
we_do.H: Explain why a flood defence does not remove carbon dioxide already added by burning fuel.

tiers.H: Compare an emissions cut with an adaptation.

stems.M: Burning ___ adds ___; this leads to ___ because ___.
stems.H: Action A changes ___, while action B helps with ___; I would choose ___ because ___.

tiers.go_deeper: Why might a council cut fuel use and plan flood defences? Name a limit of each.
tiers.early_finisher: Choose a council goal, justify the first action and explain the problem still left.

adaptations.cognition_learning: Use four large chain cards with the first and last fixed, then remove a cue.
adaptations.communication_interaction: Let partners rehearse an M/H because sentence while pointing to the chain.
adaptations.semh: Give a quiet choice of two card roles and a pause signal before the hinge.
adaptations.sensory_physical: Provide large high-contrast cards and a stable board; accept voice capture of the ordering.
adaptations.eal: Teach gas, cause and impact with arrows. Plan in any language; use M/H frames and keep the comparison challenge.

Action A changes ___, while action B helps with ___; I would choose ___ because ___.

ta_focus.i_do: Watch me place cause before effect.

ta_focus.independent: Point to your first link. Which part can you explain on your own?

prompt_ladder: Point to the lesson’s diagram, kit or source.
Ask: What is done, and what is the next step?

F.a: More heat or a greater flood risk, in some places.

M.q: What is added to the air when fuel burns?
What does a greenhouse gas do?
M.a: It slows heat loss from Earth.

H.q: How do emissions cuts and flood defences differ?
H.a: One limits the cause; the other helps with an impact.

H.q: Why does a hot day alone not prove a climate trend?
H.a: Climate is a pattern over many years.

interactions.answer_key: Correct sequence as listed; buttons give live feedback.
Flood barrier is adaptation to an impact; the others can cut emissions.

diagrams.alt: Sunlight reaches Earth. Heat leaves Earth; some heat is retained when greenhouse gases including added carbon dioxide reduce heat loss. A fuel-burning source adds carbon dioxide to air. Simplified mechanism; not to scale.
diagrams.caption: Light comes in. Earth releases heat. More CO₂ slows heat loss. Simplified mechanism; not to scale.

practical.prediction: Will ice on dark and light card melt alike?
method: Put equal ice pieces on cards in trays.
Place both trays in the same light.
Observe both at one set time.
Record what you see. Say why this is not a climate model.
results_table: Time | dark card ice | light card ice
practical.risk: Check against the school risk assessment and CLEAPSS guidance. Dry spills; use no heat source. This surface observation is not proof of the greenhouse effect.
practical.pupil_risk: Melted ice can leave a slippery spill.
practical.pupil_safety: Keep ice in trays. Wipe spills and use no heater.

facts.claim: Greenhouse gases slow heat loss and added concentrations contribute to current warming.
facts.source: NASA Science, Causes of Climate Change, https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/causes/; Met Office, Causes of Climate Change, https://weather.metoffice.gov.uk/climate-change/causes-of-climate-change

facts.claim: Current warming is not explained by the Sun alone.
facts.source: NASA Science, Causes of Climate Change, https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/causes/

facts.claim: Climate is a longer-term pattern; one day of weather does not establish a climate trend.
Warming can affect heat and rainfall patterns and raise risks in some places.
facts.source: Met Office, Effects of Climate Change, https://weather.metoffice.gov.uk/climate-change/effects-of-climate-change

facts.claim: Reducing emissions limits warming while adaptation reduces harm from impacts.
The ice-on-card task only tests a local observation and cannot model the greenhouse effect by itself.
facts.source: Inference from the task design; NASA Science, Causes of Climate Change, https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/causes/

stages: Arrival (5 min): Sort these: weather today; climate over many years. Point to the long-term idea. Staff: Offer a predictable seat or standing spot and the first visual cue. No public test.
Starter (3 min): Think back. Say, point or write one answer for each question. Staff: Ask three low-stakes retrieval questions; prior coverage must be checked.

I Do (5 min): I order the chain: burn fuel → more carbon dioxide → more heat stays → warming. Cutting emissions acts near the start. A flood defence helps with an impact. Staff: Model the full reasoning step, pre-teach four words and ask the show-me question.

We Do (7 min): The burn fuel and impact cards are in place. Sort the missing gas and warming cards. Explain the link. Staff: Show the part-done example, then allow paired talk before an answer. One-minute reset inside this stage.
We Do 2 (5 min): Choose what follows burning more fossil fuel in our warming chain. Everyone answers together. Staff: All pupils answer the four-option hinge; use the decision rule, not a score.

Independent (8 min): Build a cause-to-impact chain. Compare an emissions cut with help for an impact. Give one reason for each. Staff: One adult supports agreed pupils, the other holds the group; swap across the week. One-minute reset inside this stage.
Review (4 min): Hear feedback. Move one chain card and say why. Staff: Give a specific verbal comment (VF) and invite one self-edit (//) or read-back (?).
Exit (3 min): Name a cause, an effect and an action. Which link does your action change? Staff: Hear the answer and name how it changes the next example or support. One-minute reset and handoff.
